AN.title: ANSYS Hall
summary: ANSYS Hall is a four story, 36,000 square foot mixed-use building that incorporates a maker assembly space with immediate access to the outdoor Maker Courtyard, student collaboration space, classrooms and offices.

On the first floor of this building is TechSpark, which you can see into. This facility is a 16,000 square foot makerspace that provides resources, certification, classes and equipment for rapidly prototyping designs from ideas to reality for educational, extracurricular, and research activities. It is a hands-on learning and exploration space available to all current CMU students, faculty and staff. In addition to the highbay area for projects, the makerspace supports machining, wood working, embedded electronics, additive manufacturing, molding and casting with a dedicated wood shop, metal shop, professional shop with welding, hot metals room with jewelry making and metal casting, polymer casting room, computer lab with suite of engineering software, and a fabrication shop with 15 3D printers, 6 laser cutters and a sewing center.

Home of CMU's TechSpark macro-scale makerspace for the College of Engineering. Opened October 2019, 36,000 sq ft, four stories, designed by Bohlin Cywinski Jackson (the firm behind Apple's flagship stores and Pixar HQ) with CMU School of Architecture alumni Gregory Mottola and Kent Suhrbier leading. Funded by a naming gift from simulation-software company ANSYS, Inc. and LEED Gold certified in 2021. The signature feature is a glass high-bay with a literal garage door that rolls open onto the outdoor Maker Courtyard, letting students haul out solar-powered boats, Formula SAE racecars, and 20-foot steel bridges built by civil-engineering capstone teams. Upstairs, the ANSYS Simulation Lab overlooks the high bay, where undergrads model fluid dynamics and heat transfer using the same software sold to Boeing and Lockheed. The building anchors CMU's "Maker Ecosystem" — nano-scale fabrication in Scott Hall, component-scale in Hamerschlag, and macro-scale prototypes here. 18+ courses use the space each semester. Clubs like Carnegie Mellon Racing, the Robotics Club, and the Penguins-sponsored "Rethink the Rink" helmet-design team work here around the clock. No dining inside; Rothberg's Roasters in Scott Hall and La Prima in Gates are both a three-minute walk.

ANSYS Hall centers innovation, with a flexible high bay, laboratories, and collaboration areas that open onto an outdoor maker court. The 36,000 square-foot project serves as a connective framework — acting as a physical bridge between the surrounding buildings while bringing together multiple academic departments, ANSYS Inc., and extracurricular groups.

Centrally located and highly visible, this campus hub for making employs ample use of glass, providing layers of transparency and visual connection to foster interdisciplinary exchange. Wherever you are within the building, you can enjoy views of bustling activity occurring in other spaces. When walking across the elevated outdoor bridge, campus visitors catch glimpses of undergraduates assembling full-scale prototypes in the high bay below. In turn, students working in the high bay enjoy views to the ANSYS Simulation Room where colleagues experiment with the ANSYS software — simulating interactions for physics, structures, vibration, fluid dynamics, heat transfer, and electromagnetics. The facility allows ANSYS, Inc. and students to collaborate openly and freely while providing ANSYS, Inc. with a secure office suite. Ensuring a long-term academic-corporate partnership, ANSYS Hall creates an environment where students learn and test cutting-edge simulation software, provide direct feedback to the manufacturer, and create a pipeline for future industry employment and leadership.

ANSYS Hall marks a new gateway at the southwest corner of campus, a strikingly contemporary response integrated within the historic Hornbostel-designed buildings. It is the final link to the College of Engineering "Maker Ecosystem" that includes nano-, micro-, and macro-fabrication, bringing together undergraduate and graduate students from multiple disciplines in a hands-on environment that encourages and displays the cross-pollination of ideas and innovation. The iconic design responds to the underlying principles of the existing architecture and campus context while offering a high-performing, adaptable space.

BH.title: Baker Hall
summary: Baker Hall is one of the oldest buildings on campus and connects to Porter Hall via a long, sloped hallway. Baker is home to the Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences. Our humanities are situated at the intersection of humanity and technology. For undergraduates, Dietrich houses 37 majors that are designed to be completed in 2 years, which allows students to add on additional majors, minors, and dual degrees. With this flexibility comes the ability to participate in experiences including internships, research, study abroad and more to prepare their students for the next step on their journey of graduate school or a career.

Built in 1914 and 1919 as the original Administration Hall (also known as Central Building), Baker is the classroom-and-office anchor of the Marianna Brown Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences — renamed in September 2011 after a historic $265 million gift from CMU trustee William S. Dietrich II to honor his late mother, the homemaker who inspired him; it was among the 10 largest gifts to U.S. private higher education at the time. It houses English, History, Philosophy, Psychology, Social & Decision Sciences, Statistics & Data Science, and Pre-Law Advising. Designed by Henry Hornbostel's Palmer & Hornbostel firm, its signature feature is the long sloping main corridor that continues into Porter Hall with no stairs — designed so the building could be converted into a factory if Carnegie Tech failed as a university. Inside you'll find Guastavino tile vaulting, a signature spiral red-stone staircase, and a polished bronze bust of Andrew Carnegie. Giant Eagle Auditorium (BH A51) — named for the Pittsburgh grocery chain — is the big-lecture venue, and the Adamson Wing and Baker Cluster computer lab draw steady traffic. Dining is Ginger's Express on the lower level. The legendary student prank is "chairing" — riding an office chair down the sloped corridor, officially discouraged but culturally inescapable. The faculty legacy is remarkable: this was the administrative home of Herbert Simon (1978 Nobel in Economics, 1975 Turing Award), who helped found both CMU's Psychology Department and its School of Computer Science. Other Nobel laureates tied to Dietrich include Oliver Williamson (2009), Finn Kydland, and Edward Prescott (2004). CMU's cognitive psychology program ranks #5 nationally.

CFA.title: College of Fine Arts
summary: College of Fine Arts Building is an architectural creation of Henry Hornbostel, the college’s first dean, and is home to three of its five schools: architecture, art, and music. To speak a little more about each of these:
It includes the school of Music, Art, and Architecture

The CFA building is Henry Hornbostel's tribute to his own education at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris — cornerstone laid April 25, 1912, building completed in 1917. The College of Fine Arts itself was founded in 1905 as one of the first comprehensive fine-arts colleges in the United States; its five schools — Architecture, Art, Design, Drama, and Music — were formally consolidated under that structure by 1995. The cream-brick Beaux-Arts façade features five exterior niches with reliefs representing Greek, Roman, Medieval, Renaissance, and non-Western stylistic periods, but only the Renaissance niche was carved when the building opened in 1917. The other four sat empty for nearly 70 years, until alumnus Verner S. Purnell (CMU 1926) funded their completion in 1987; carving was executed 1990–1993 by an international team of stone masons led by Nicholas Fairplay, Bruce Lindsey, and Paul Rosenblatt and described at the time as "the most important stonework project underway in North America." In the Roman niche above the entrance, a bust of Bacchus is carved with Hornbostel's own face, paired with a bust of Mercury depicting Verner S. Purnell himself. The Great Hall's marble floors display embedded plans of the world's great historical monuments so students literally walk over architectural history; the vaulted ceiling murals — painted by James Hewlett — include a depiction of Hornbostel's own Hell Gate Bridge in New York. Kresge Theatre (255 seats) is the recital and convocation venue; Alumni Concert Hall serves large ensembles. No dining inside, but Ginger's Express in Purnell and The Exchange in Posner are steps away. The alumni list is the tour-app headliner. School of Art: Andy Warhol (Pictorial Design, 1949), Philip Pearlstein, Mel Bochner, John Currin, Jonathan Borofsky. School of Drama (founded 1914, the oldest degree-granting drama program in the U.S., admit rate under 3% in recent years versus ~18% for the College of Fine Arts overall): Ted Danson, Holly Hunter, Ethan Hawke, Jeff Goldblum, Zachary Quinto, Patrick Wilson, Matt Bomer, Josh Gad, Josh Groban, Leslie Odom Jr., Billy Porter, Judith Light, Christian Borle, Rob Marshall, Steven Bochco. Music: Stephen Schwartz (composer of Wicked), Keith Lockhart (Boston Pops). Hornbostel himself wore red satin string ties, kept a pet monkey, and drove a convertible with his dog as co-pilot.

DH.title: Doherty Hall
summary: Doherty Hall contains some of the largest lecture style classrooms and renovated lab spaces for our Mellon College of Science students, in addition to lab and studio spaces for departments like Engineering, Chemistry, Biology and Art.

The Mellon College of Science houses 4 departments with 20 majors including biology, chemistry, physics, mathematics. Over 70% of undergraduates in this college do research. The college facilities also include a Cloud Lab that is the first academic Cloud Laboratory in the country and home to programmable robot-run experimentation instruments.

Also the new Richard King Mellon Hall of Sciences is coming in 2027 that will house our Mellon College of Science, the university's School of Computer Science and the public Institute for Contemporary Art. This mix of science, technology and art will spur exciting opportunities for cross-collaboration and embody Carnegie's Mellon spirit of innovation.

Built in 1908 as the School of Applied Sciences, Doherty anchors Hornbostel's "Mall" and houses Mellon College of Science's Chemistry and Biological Sciences departments alongside College of Engineering's Chemical Engineering (continuously there since 1908). Named for trustee Henry L. Doherty. The Phase II addition (2009, LEED Silver) added three green roofs, including a semi-intensive roof with a bluestone-and-beach-pebble spiral walkway above C-level that doubles as an outdoor classroom. Doherty's defining quirk: no two floors have identical layouts, you cannot walk from the front of the first floor to the back without detouring, and the third and fourth floors exist only in two small towers that don't connect to each other. The maze continues into Wean Hall via five different stair/hallway connections — a rite of passage for every first-year trying to find class. Five large interdisciplinary teaching labs serve chemistry and chem-E students; 90% of chemistry majors do undergraduate research. No dining inside; La Prima in Gates or Stephanie's in the Mellon Institute are closest. Clarifying the original brief: the CMU Cloud Lab is not located in Doherty — it's in a CMU-owned building near Bakery Square — but Doherty chemistry faculty are its primary users. In December 2023, Assistant Professor Gabe Gomes — with chemical engineering doctoral students Daniil Boiko and Robert MacKnight — published a Nature paper on "Coscientist," an AI system using GPT-4 and Anthropic's Claude that autonomously designed, planned, and executed chemistry experiments (including optimizing palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions), leveraging the Cloud Lab's 200+ instruments running 24/7. Doherty's role will shift when the 338,900-sq-ft Richard King Mellon Hall of Sciences opens in 2027 — a roughly $300 million project (initial estimate $252M) anchored by a $75 million lead grant from the Richard King Mellon Foundation as part of a $150M partnership, designed by Portland's ZGF Architects with local R3A Architecture, with construction managed by a PJ Dick / Mascaro Construction joint venture; groundbreaking was April 12, 2024 at the corner of Forbes Avenue and South Craig Street, and the building will house the Mellon College of Science, parts of the School of Computer Science, and the Institute for Contemporary Art Pittsburgh.

GHC.title: Gates and Hillman Centers
summary: Gates and Hillman Centers for Future-Generation Technologies are home to the School of Computer Science and Computational Biology Department. These Gold LEED Certified Centers were made possible by lead gifts from the Bill and Melinda Gates and the Henry L. Hillman foundations. The building also houses a Mission Control Center for the student project Iris Rover created by over 300 students from across the university that was the first of its kind to survive a launch and a zero-gravity environment.

The School of Computer Science was the first standalone school of Computer Science in the nation and launched the first Artificial Intelligence degree by a US University. The school houses five undergraduate majors including Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Computational Biology, Human Computer Interaction, Robotics.

Completed in 2009 and dedicated September 22, 2009, GHC is the home of the School of Computer Science at 4902 Forbes Avenue. It's 217,000 sq ft across nine stories, designed by Mack Scogin Merrill Elam Architects, LEED Gold certified, built with a $20 million gift from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and $10 million from the Hillman Foundation. A cistern captures 500,000 gallons of rain and snowmelt per year for toilet flushing, and 98% of construction waste (19,000 tons) was diverted from landfill. The building won a 2012 AIA Institute Honor Award for Architecture, one of just nine worldwide that year. The complex navigates an unusually steep 75-foot site-elevation change, and the signature feature is The Helix — a long spiral ramp inside the Gates atrium that traverses several stories, famous for unofficial student stunts including mountain-bike descents and office-chair races. The black zinc diamond-shingle cladding is a modern reinterpretation of Hornbostel's brick; each of 310+ windows has its own silver zinc surround. The Randy Pausch Memorial Bridge to Purnell features 7,000+ programmable LED lights and symbolically links computer science to drama — Pausch taught both. Its opening lighting sequences depicted six visual metaphors from his book "The Last Lecture" (Fun with Crayons, Outer Space, Make the Most of Each Day, Be the First Penguin, The Elevator in Randy's Room, Disney and the Circus), and abstract penguin cut-outs in the bridge's structure honor his "first penguin" message. Rashid Auditorium seats 250; its seats carry a cryptic binary pattern long rumored by students to be ASCII (analysts confirmed it's not). Other named spaces include the Luis von Ahn "Awesome Classroom" (gift of the Duolingo and reCAPTCHA founder, CS '03/'05), the Raj Reddy Conference Room, and the Moonshot Mission Control for lunar rover missions. Dining is Rohr Café on floor 3 — espresso, sandwiches, and a popular study spot with one of the healthier menus on campus. The Iris Rover launched January 8, 2024 aboard Astrobotic's Peregrine lander on the maiden flight of the Vulcan Centaur rocket. Built by 300+ students at just 4 pounds and shoebox-sized, Iris was billed as the first American, first university-developed, smallest, and lightest robotic lunar rover. Important accuracy note: the Peregrine lander suffered a propellant leak hours after launch and never reached the Moon, burning up over the Pacific on January 18, 2024 — but Iris successfully powered on and communicated from space, and a replica is displayed at the Smithsonian. Turing Award winners Raj Reddy, Manuel Blum, and Edmund M. Clarke are associated with the building, alongside pioneers Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, Randy Pausch ("The Last Lecture"), and former faculty member Geoffrey Hinton (2024 Nobel in Physics).

HBH.title: Hamburg Hall
summary: Built 1915–1917 by Henry Hornbostel as the main building of the U.S. Bureau of Mines Central Experiment Station, Hamburg was acquired by CMU in 1984–1985 (U.S. Senator H. John Heinz III was instrumental) and is on the National Register of Historic Places since 1974. Today it's the headquarters of Heinz College — CMU's dual School of Public Policy & Management and School of Information Systems & Management. A 2013–2017, $18M+ renovation by GBBN Architects, funded by a $10M gift from The Heinz Endowments, inserted a 150-seat glass-enclosed auditorium into the former courtyard between Hamburg and Smith Halls, achieving LEED Gold for that phase. The Hamburg Hall 1000 rotunda was reimagined as a grand lobby, and a 3,600-sq-ft rooftop plaza sits above the new auditorium.

Heinz College has ~1,500 students and operated a branch campus in Adelaide, Australia from 2006 until it was wound down following a June 2022 announcement (over 1,200 students completed degrees through the Adelaide campus during its 16-year run). Weekly speakers have included Senator Bob Casey, former San Juan Mayor Carmen Yulín Cruz (MSPPM '86), Martin O'Malley, MoMA Director Glenn Lowry, and author Ijeoma Oluo. The school was renamed for Senator Heinz in 1992 following his 1991 death, with a lead gift from Teresa Heinz. Current Dean: Kirsten Martin (the H. John Heinz III Dean of the Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy; her research focuses on technology ethics and algorithmic accountability). Notable faculty include Alessandro Acquisti (privacy economics) and Jonathan Caulkins (drug policy). Alumna Leah Lizarondo founded Pittsburgh's 412 Food Rescue.

HH.title: Hamerschlag Hall
summary: Hamerschlag Hall is home to Electrical & Computer Engineering. The building's rotunda is one of the most iconic images on campus. This building also boasts a living roof

Hornbostel's 1912 Machinery Hall — renamed in 1964 for Arthur A. Hamerschlag, first president of Carnegie Technical Schools (1903–1922) — is home to the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (450 undergrads, 300 grads) plus Mechanical Engineering labs and College of Engineering classrooms. The iconic feature is the domed round tower, a functional ~64-foot smokestack disguising the old power plant's flue and often called "the most beautiful smokestack ever created." Hornbostel designed the building as "the helm of an explorer's ship" pointing toward the Carnegie Institute, with a perfect axial view to Pitt's Cathedral of Learning. The entrance features a copy of the U.S.S. Pittsburgh cruiser's bow ornament. The cream-colored Kittanning brick was Hornbostel's deliberate signal of "practical, modern" identity versus red-brick Ivy League schools. Inside sits the HH-1107 Undergraduate Computer Cluster (recently upgraded as a makerspace), the Additive Manufacturing Lab, and the historic cleanroom facilities — though most nanofabrication has migrated to the Eden Hall Foundation Cleanroom — roughly 8,500 sq ft of Class 10/100 cleanroom inside the larger Bertucci Nanotechnology Laboratory in the adjacent Sherman and Joyce Bowie Scott Hall (which opened April 30, 2016, with the cleanroom fully operational in 2017). In 2016, Volpatt Construction replaced 68 historic wood single-pane windows with custom-matched profiles. The tower is CMU's single most recognizable visual icon, appearing on nearly every postcard and promotional image. (Don't confuse Hamerschlag Hall with Hamerschlag House, a separate first-year residence nicknamed "Schlag" that was renovated in 2024–2025.)

HL.title: Hunt Library
summary: Dedicated October 10, 1961, Hunt is CMU's main library and its only purpose-built library — the $2.8 million gift of Roy A. Hunt (an Alcoa founder, hence the aluminum-and-glass exterior) and his wife Rachel McMasters Miller Hunt, a legendary rare-book collector. Designed by Lawrie & Green, its cantilevered canopy names the donors on one side and the Rachel Hunt Botanical Library on the other, and nighttime LED illumination makes it glow from across The Cut. Five floors plus an A-level basement. The fifth-floor penthouse houses the Hunt Institute for Botanical Documentation — Rachel's personal rare-book legacy including medieval vellum manuscripts on medicinal herbs and Maria Sibylla Merian botanical books, "arguably the best collection of botanical books ever assembled by an individual in this country." The fourth floor has the Fine & Rare Book Room (600+ artists' books). The basement houses IDeATe — Integrative Design, Arts, and Technology — CMU's fabrication, media, physical computing, and soft technologies labs offering nine undergraduate minors fusing art and tech. The third floor is the dead-silent quiet floor, and the Hunt Library Gallery is currently hosting "Room to Imagine: 125 Years of Carnegie Mellon University" (Sept 11, 2025 – July 10, 2026) — curated by Julia Corrin with art director Heidi Wiren Kébé and editorial director Brad King — an immersive installation built into the form of a college dorm room and tracing CMU innovations from the iPhone interface (Freddy Anzures) to Toy Story (Ralph Guggenheim), Duolingo (Luis von Ahn), and Silly Putty (Earl Warrick), with a companion "Imagination to Innovation" section displaying toys designed by alumni. Dining is the Maggie Murph Café on the first floor, operated since fall 2022 by De Fer Coffee & Tea — a Pittsburgh specialty roastery founded in 2016 by CMU alumnus Matt Marietti (Tepper MBA '10) and his wife Vanessa, with six locations across Pittsburgh (flagship in the Strip District, where they roast in-house daily). Extended hours run Mon–Fri 8 a.m. to 3 a.m., and during finals weekends extend to 3 a.m. as well — valid CMU ID required after 7 p.m.

HOA.title: Hall of the Arts
summary: Hall of the Arts (HOA) is a four-story academic building on Carnegie Mellon's campus, located on the Forbes Avenue side near Posner Hall and the rest of the campus arts corridor (Margaret Morrison, Purnell, CFA). Originally designed by Henry Hornbostel, the building's exterior buff-colored brick facade was preserved through its most recent renovation.

The building was originally constructed as the home of the Graduate School of Industrial Administration (GSIA) and most recently housed the Tepper School of Business until Tepper relocated to Tepper Quad in 2018. (Note: Posner Hall, which sits adjacent, was the 1990–1993 GSIA expansion building — not the original. Both housed Tepper before the move.)
A multi-phased gut renovation completed in 2020–2021 transformed the interior into a major facility for the College of Fine Arts. The renovated Hall of the Arts opened in 2020.

The School of Music occupies most of three floors of the four-story building. Denis G. Colwell, Jack G. Buncher Head of the School of Music, called it 'the most significant expansion of space the School of Music has had since it was founded.' Music facilities in HOA include: 13 instrument-dedicated studios, two chamber music rehearsal rooms, three new music classrooms, a music technology room and recording suite, 25 faculty offices (with 50 faculty members now having offices or studios specific to their instrument), and two conference rooms.
The top floor of Hall of the Arts is home to the School of Art's Master of Fine Arts (MFA) Program.

HOA also houses standard registrar-controlled classrooms — notably HOA 107 and HOA 160 — used by classes from across the university and equipped with wireless presenting technology, making it a regular destination for students from many majors taking elective coursework.

Important disambiguation: HOA is distinct from the historic College of Fine Arts (CFA) building, also Hornbostel-designed, on the opposite side of campus. CFA houses the Schools of Architecture, Art, and Music administrative spaces along with the Kresge Theatre and Alumni Concert Hall. If a student's schedule lists 'HOA,' they should head to the building near Posner Hall — not to the CFA building with the famous niches and Great Hall.

MM.title: Margaret Morrison Carnegie Hall
summary: Margaret Morrison Carnegie Hall, affectionately known on campus as 'Maggie Mo'. This building originally housed the Margaret Morrison Carnegie College for Women, and it now houses some years of the design and architecture programs as well as our on campus children’s school!

The School of Design is an exploration of humanity and sustainable systems. With a focus on interdisciplinary learning, our programs prepare students for real-world design challenges by working collaboratively across fields. CMU was the first school to offer a degree in Industrial Design. Now it’s called “Product Design”.

Built 1906– 1907 by Henry Hornbostel as the Margaret Morrison Carnegie School for Women — CMU's original women's college, named for Andrew Carnegie's mother — this is now the home of the School of Design (CFA) plus parts of the School of Architecture, including the renowned Center for Building Performance and Diagnostics. Alumnae were called "Maggie Murphs." The women's college closed in 1973 due to declining enrollment as CMU fully integrated. The signature feature is the grand semicircular colonnaded rotunda with inscribed dedication from 1907 (you'll see references to both Ionic and Doric column orders across sources — the SAH Archipedia says Doric). Inside the rotunda, alumna Rebecca Deutsch ('04) installed stenciled quotes from women students across CMU history, responding to the original inscription. The rooftop hosts the Robert L. Preger Intelligent Workplace — a 7,000-sq-ft shimmering glass penthouse added in 1997 as an internationally recognized green-building research lab that predates LEED certification. A 1990–1996 Bohlin Cywinski Jackson renovation updated the interior. Hornbostel originally intended a matching rear wing with a second rotunda; it was never built. Notable alumna: Stephanie Kwolek (MMCC '46) — inventor of Kevlar.

NSH.title: Newell-Simon Hall
summary: Newell-Simon Hall (NSH) is a six-story academic building located in the northwestern part of Carnegie Mellon's campus, adjacent to Wean Hall (which connects to NSH via a skyway bridge on Wean's 4th floor).

The building is named after Herbert A. Simon and Allen Newell, two CMU professors who were pioneers of artificial intelligence and cognitive science. Simon and Newell shared the 1975 ACM Turing Award for their contributions to AI and the psychology of human cognition. Simon additionally won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his pioneering research on decision-making within economic organizations. Together they developed some of the earliest AI programs at CMU in the late 1950s, including the Logic Theorist (often considered the first artificial intelligence program) and the General Problem Solver.

NSH was originally constructed in 1934 and was built atop two earlier buildings (Buildings C and D) acquired from the United States Bureau of Mines, which had a major Pittsburgh experiment station on the site.
The building houses three of the School of Computer Science's flagship units: the Robotics Institute, the Human-Computer Interaction Institute (HCII), and the Quality of Life Technology Center.

The Robotics Institute, founded in October 1979 by President Dick Cyert, Raj Reddy, and Angel Jordan with support from Westinghouse Corporation, was the first academic department in the world devoted exclusively to robotics. Raj Reddy served as its founding director from 1979 to 1991, and the Institute introduced the world's first Ph.D. program in robotics in 1988.

A major renovation and addition project for the Robotics Institute portion of NSH was designed by NEXT architecture and completed at a cost of approximately $5.8 million. The project added 25,000 square feet of renovated teaching labs and collaboration space, plus a cantilevered conference room overlooking the Robotics Institute high bay. It achieved LEED Silver certification with 80% of construction waste diverted from landfills. Notable renovation challenges included an uneven first floor that required slab leveling, extensive mechanical upgrades, and a mysterious water reservoir discovered behind a first-floor wall.

About the namesakes: Allen Newell (1927–1992) was a CMU computer science and cognitive psychology professor, recipient of the 1975 Turing Award (with Simon) and the 1992 IEEE Emanuel R. Piore Award. Herbert A. Simon (1916–2001) was a CMU professor across multiple disciplines (Computer Science, Psychology, Economics, Public Policy), recipient of the 1975 Turing Award and the 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, and is considered one of the founders of the fields of artificial intelligence, cognitive psychology, and behavioral economics.

PCA.title: Purnell Center for the Arts
summary: Purnell Center for the Arts is home to our School of Drama, the nation’s oldest degree-granting drama program, and includes state-of-the-art performance and education facilities like the Philip Chosky Theater and the Regina Gouger Miller Gallery. Whether you see yourself on stage, behind the scenes, or forging a creative path all on your own, our School of Drama’s specialized curriculum and dedicated, world-class faculty can help you get there with majors in acting/musical theater, design, dramaturgy, and production technology & management.

Opened in 2000 and named for alumnus-donor Verner S. Purnell, Purnell is home to the School of Drama — the oldest degree-granting drama program in the United States (founded 1914) — plus the Miller Institute for Contemporary Art. Approximately 110,000 sq ft, designed by the DDF Associates joint venture (Michael Dennis and Associates with theatre specialist John Sergio Fisher AIA, plus local firm Damianos + Anthony) in a neoclassical style with a rotunda lobby mirroring Margaret Morrison's across campus. Admit rate for the drama program is under 3% in recent years — the lowest at CMU. Philip Chosky Theater is the ~500-seat proscenium mainstage (convertible to thrust), featuring a 24′×18′ trap door section, tension grid, motorized orchestra pit, and computerized rigging — it replaced the 90-year-old Kresge Theatre. Helen Wayne Rauh Studio Theatre is the 130–140-seat flexible black-box. The building also houses the John Wells Video Studio (three-camera TV sound stage), a world-renowned lighting lab, and two dance studios. Miller ICA is a free, three-story, 8,000-sq-ft contemporary gallery founded in 2000 by alumna Regina Gouger Miller; it hosts the annual MFA Exhibition and BFA/BXA Senior Shows. The signature student tradition is "Playground: A Festival of Independent Student Work," running for 20+ years — the School of Drama cancels all classes for the week while students propose, produce, and perform 60+ original works across three days, spanning new plays, musical performances, lighting and art installations, murals, and multimedia projects. Notable Playground alumni include Patina Miller (Broadway's "Sister Act"), Josh Gad ("The Book of Mormon"), and Amanda Jane Cooper ("Wicked" national tour); the PigPen Theatre Company first performed together at Playground in 2007 before going on to win Best of the New York International Fringe Festival and compose the music for Broadway's "Water for Elephants." The alumni roll is legendary: Ted Danson, Holly Hunter, Zachary Quinto, Josh Groban, Patrick Wilson, Steven Bochco, Ethan Hawke, Sutton Foster, Megan Hilty, Cherry Jones, Judith Light, Rob Marshall, Billy Porter, Leslie Odom Jr., Renée Elise Goldsberry, Christian Borle. CMU alumni have won numerous major industry honors including 66 Tony Awards, 99+ Emmys, and 13 Academy Awards. On April 28, 2014 — coinciding with the School of Drama's centennial — CMU became the first and exclusive higher-education partner of the Tony Awards, co-creating the "Tony Honor for Excellence in Theatre Education presented by Carnegie Mellon University," the first national recognition program for K–12 theatre educators (introduced on the June 8, 2014 broadcast by CMU alumni Zachary Quinto and Matt Bomer; first recipient honored at the 2015 Tony Awards).

PH.title: Porter Hall
summary: Porter Hall is the first building constructed on the CMU campus, an original Henry Hornbostel design in his signature Beaux-Arts style and Kittanning cream brick. It connects directly to Baker Hall via a famously long sloped corridor — both buildings were designed with flat sloped corridors instead of stairs so the structures could be converted to factory use if Carnegie Tech had failed as a university.

Today Porter is home to several of CMU's interdisciplinary programs, including the Department of Engineering and Public Policy (EPP) — a uniquely CMU dual-degree program where engineering students pair their major with policy coursework. Porter also houses some of the most heavily used undergraduate lecture halls on campus (rooms commonly numbered Porter A18, A19, and A22), drawing classes from across many departments.

Porter Hall is the very first building built on our campus. It is connected to Baker Hall and is home to interdisciplinary programs. One interesting fact about this building is that when it was originally built it featured two entrances — the bottom entrance was used for students, and the top, more ornately decorated entrance was used for faculty members.

SH.title: Scaife Hall
summary: Alan Magee Scaife Hall of Engineering is a new 85,000 square-foot building comprising labs, a drone arena, offices, classrooms, and a café. The labs support research in a variety of subjects ranging from Biology to Robotics to Rapid Prototyping and are supported by 100 PhD workspaces directly adjacent to the lab spaces. The building is the home for the Mechanical Engineering Department.

Grand opening was November 9–10, 2023 for the new 85,000-sq-ft Scaife — double the size of the original 1962 building (the famous "Potato Chip" auditorium, demolished 2020). Named for benefactor Alan Magee Scaife. Designed by Philadelphia firm KieranTimberlake, with lead funding from the Allegheny Foundation. The building is the home of the Department of Mechanical Engineering and uses 25% less energy than the ASHRAE 90.1-2010 baseline, with 43% offset by CMU's off-site wind farm and a net pEUI of 77 kBtu/sf. The adjacent plaza was dedicated at opening as the Gordon E. Moore Engineering Quad, honoring the Intel co-founder.

The signature feature is a double-height high-bay drone/UAV arena whose floor is patterned specifically to aid motion-capture data capture — viewable from the circulation space above. Inside: 11 research labs across levels A and B (wet labs, dry labs, robotics, biosafety level 1, rapid prototyping, tissue culturing), about 100 PhD workspaces, 80+ offices, 19 meeting rooms, and a green rooftop garden connecting to ANSYS Hall's TechSpark via large operable doors. Public art installation "Making Way" by Jessica Stockholder was commissioned to match the building's "breaking boundaries" theme. Views from the Engineering Quad extend to Junction Hollow, Schenley Park, and Pitt's Cathedral of Learning. Dining is Redhawk Coffee on the first floor, opened fall 2023 with a September 28 grand opening. Redhawk is a Pittsburgh family-owned roastery; the CMU menu includes Driftwood Oven pastries, matcha lattes, mochas with Brunton's chocolate milk, and a signature honey-cinnamon latte. Fun fact: the original 1962 Scaife's state-of-the-art computer occupied the entire fourth floor, had to be carried in by helicopter, and had less processing power than a modern smartphone.

Standing as a grand "cornerstone" of Carnegie Mellon's campus, the new Alan Magee Scaife Hall of Engineering is an 85,000-square-foot marvel completed in 2023. Replacing the original 1962 structure, this six-story facility serves as a primary entrance to the university at Frew Street, offering stunning views of Junction Hollow and Schenley Park. Architecture students will appreciate its unique three-part design: a two-story "podium" built directly into the hillside, a four-story south mass, and a two-story north mass that features a specialized portal designed specifically to allow emergency vehicles to pass through to Hamerschlag Drive.

Innovation in Action: For those interested in the future of technology, Scaife Hall is the powerhouse of the Mechanical Engineering Department. It isn't just a place for lectures; it houses a high-bay drone arena and 11 specialized labs ranging from robotics to rapid prototyping and biology. The building is designed for "intellectual vitality," featuring 19 meeting rooms, a 200-seat lecture hall, and over 100 PhD workspaces positioned directly adjacent to the labs. When students aren't busy with research, they can be found collaborating in the common areas or grabbing a coffee at the building's on-site café.

A Model of Sustainability: CMU has a deep commitment to the environment, and Scaife Hall is on track for LEED Gold certification. The building is a living classroom for sustainability; it uses 24% less energy than similar buildings and has reduced its indoor water consumption by a staggering 36% — saving over 170,000 gallons of water annually. Even the landscaping is smart, featuring a green roof and bio-retention areas that manage stormwater not just for Scaife, but also for the neighboring Baker and Porter Halls. To keep the air fresh, the building utilizes CO2 sensors that automatically cycle in outdoor air whenever it's needed.

Community and Circularity: The story of this building actually began with what was taken away — before the old Scaife Hall was demolished, CMU donated 11 tons of materials like doors and furniture to local nonprofits. During construction, the team diverted 75% of waste — about 2,500 tons — from landfills. Today, the facility encourages a "green" lifestyle by providing extensive bicycle facilities and easy access to public transit. Inside, you'll find zero-mercury LED lighting and building materials that are "red-list free," meaning they don't contain chemicals harmful to humans, ensuring a healthy environment for the next generation of engineers.

TCS.title: TCS Hall
summary: Accuracy note: TCS Hall opened April 21, 2020 (not 2023), but it remains one of CMU's newest academic buildings. Dedicated in a ceremony with Governor Tom Wolf, Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran, and President Farnam Jahanian. Funded by a $35 million gift from Tata Consultancy Services in 2015 — at the time, the largest industry and international donation in CMU history — the gift also funds 17+ student fellowships and 20+ capstone projects. Roughly 90,000 sq ft on 5 stories above a ground-floor parking garage, LEED Gold certified, designed by Bohlin Cywinski Jackson (Gregory Mottola and Kent Suhrbier, both CMU architecture alumni). Located at 4615 Forbes Avenue, it's the first major building north of Forbes and serves as CMU's literal front door from Forbes Avenue. The building houses the Institute for Software Research (Software and Societal Systems, S3D) of the School of Computer Science, the Master of Science in Computational Finance (MSCF) program, the University Business Engagement Center, and TCS Pace Port Pittsburgh — TCS's fourth global co-innovation hub (5th floor, 8,000 sq ft), specializing in manufacturing and utilities innovation. Patterned brick, terracotta, and aluminum recall Hornbostel's historic palette in contemporary form. A two-story "Student Collaboration Porch" greets visitors; an outdoor "robot yard" and eco-sustainable rain garden sit alongside. Stephanie Dinkins' 44-foot mural "Good Thoughts, Good Words, Good Deeds" was installed in 2022. The flexible floor plates and drone high-bay make TCS the place where CS students, computational-finance quants, and engineering teams mix.
Major financial firms that recruit from the MSCF program include Citi, Bloomberg, Citadel, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank, Blackrock, AQR, Fidelity, PNC, and BNY Mellon.

TEP.title: Tepper Quad
summary: Tepper Quad Building, is a 315,000 square foot state-of-the-art building, is home to the Tepper School of Business, the Coulter Welcome Center, fitness center, dining locations, JP Morgan and Chase AI Makerspace, and the Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship.

The Tepper School of Business houses three variations of undergraduate majors including Business administration major with 9 different concentrations, Multiple ways to earn an Economics major, and a Computational Finance major.

Here at CMU we do not have a central dining hall, but 30+ different eateries around campus. Inside the Tepper Building we have Rohr Commons featuring Build Pizza, Forbes Ave Subs, Tepper Taqueria, and Millie's Coffee ‘N Creamery.

Opened September 13, 2018, the David A. Tepper Quadrangle is CMU's largest building at 315,000 sq ft across five stories — each floor is over an acre. Designed by Moore Ruble Yudell Architects (lead: Buzz Yudell) with R3A as associate architect, and built by PJ Dick for roughly $201–205 million. Funded in part by a $67 million lead gift from alumnus David A. Tepper (TPR '82) toward the building itself — Tepper, a billionaire hedge-fund founder of Appaloosa Management and owner of the Carolina Panthers (NFL) and Charlotte FC (MLS), has given CMU more than $125 million in total, including $55 million to name and endow the Tepper School. Additional lead gifts: $5M from David Coulter (TPR '71) for the welcome center and $31M from Jim Swartz (TPR '66, co-founder of Accel Partners) for the entrepreneurship center. The building is LEED Gold (73 of 79 points) with 82,000 sq ft of exterior glass giving 85% of the interior natural light, and is the first BubbleDeck building in Pennsylvania and the largest-floor-area BubbleDeck installation in the United States — the recycled-plastic balls suspended in the concrete are reportedly made from rejected plastic kayaks, reducing concrete use by 35% and embodied carbon by ~30%. A 120,000-gallon rainwater cistern serves building systems. Notable spaces: Simmons Auditorium (600 seats, CMU's largest and flat-floor reconfigurable), the Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship (15,000 sq ft with 10 startup "maker-space garages"), a 7,200-sq-ft fitness center, the JPMorgan Chase AI Maker Space, the Askwith Kenner Global Languages Room, and 24 tech-enabled classrooms. The Coulter Welcome Center is where every official CMU guided campus tour begins, led by Tartan Ambassadors 9 a.m.–4:30 p.m. daily (closed Wednesdays). Dining in Rohr Commons includes Tazza D'Oro (Pittsburgh-local coffee) and Pure (healthy bowls). In fall 2024, School of Design graduate students installed interactive updates including a miniature version of The Fence and a student-project wall. President Jahanian has called Tepper Quad CMU's "new front door to campus." A fun cultural aside: it's next door to the WQED studios where Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was filmed.

WEH.title: Wean Hall
summary: Opened 1971, renamed October 9, 1981 for industrialist Raymond "Jack" Wean (Carnegie Tech 1917), designed by Dahlen K. Ritchey for $15.5 million (1971 dollars). Wean is CMU's sole brutalist building — a massive reinforced-concrete bunker 8 stories tall, built into the side of a ravine so that only 3 stories plus a mechanical penthouse are visible from the Mall side, the remaining 5 descending into the hillside. No two floors have identical layouts. Nicknamed "The Turtle." It was Pittsburgh's largest all-concrete building after Three Rivers Stadium was imploded in 2001. Houses the Department of Mathematical Sciences, parts of the School of Computer Science (classrooms, labs, clusters), Physics labs, the Sorrells Engineering and Science Library, and Machine Learning Department offices on the subterranean level. Wean connects to Doherty through a warren of stairs and hallways at five different levels — the site of the student game "Capture the Flag with Stuff." Major facade repairs in 2013–2014 exposed and encased rusted rebar ahead of the SCS 50th anniversary. A recent lobby renovation by IKM Architecture added a glass "crystal" prism under the brutalist overhang to create a light-filled, recruitment-friendly entrance housing an expanded La Prima Espresso. Dining is La Prima Espresso Company — a staple for 30+ years, Pittsburgh's only certified organic coffee roaster, serving Italian-style espresso, nitro cold brew, Mediterra Bakehouse pastries, and curried chickpea wraps. Fun fact: students claim an unofficial world record for "most bottle caps stuck in holes in a building" — plastic bottle caps are the exact size of the form-tie holes in Wean's concrete walls. Scott Fahlman, whose office sat in the CS computing ecosystem, invented the :-) emoticon at CMU on September 19, 1982 at 11:44 AM, in a post on a CMU bulletin board proposing it as a "joke marker." The Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center (founded 1986 by CMU physicist Michael Levine) is closely affiliated with Wean's computing history.

CYH.title: Cyert Hall
summary: president Originally the University Computing Center, renamed for Richard Michael Cyert (1921–1998), CMU's 6th president from 1972–1990 and co-author of the seminal 1959 A Behavioral Theory of the Firm. Cyert's presidency transformed CMU "from an Eastern technical school to a premier American university," launching the largest expansion in school history and focusing the university on computing. The building is a workmanlike concrete mid/late-20th-century academic structure at 5000 Forbes Avenue. It houses CMU Computing Services — the university's main network infrastructure and ITS data center (rack-mount colocation, web servers, AFS/DFS/NFS storage, authentication systems); the Office of International Education (Suite 101 — study abroad advising, F-1/J-1 visas, I-20/DS-2019 issuance); the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (in a 2021 renovation of 5,730 sq ft by NEXT Architecture); Desk Services tech help (Room 119); and student computer labs. The CS Department itself was established in 1965 with a $5M Mellon grant — Alan Perlis (the very first ACM Turing Award recipient in 1966) was its first head. Cyert Hall is effectively the plumbing of CMU's digital life — the first stop for international students handling visas and for students launching study-abroad journeys.

WH.title: Warner Hall
summary: Warner Hall is home to the Office of Undergraduate Admission on the second floor. Their office is open from 8:30AM - 4:30PM Monday through Friday if you would like to stop in for a walk-in appointment.
The HUB and Enrollment Services also reside here, which would be where you get your Student ID if you choose to attend CMU.

Opened 1965–1966 and named for John Christian Warner, CMU's 4th president (1950–1965), Warner is CMU's main administrative building and sits at 5000 Forbes Avenue — the official mailing address for most of the campus. It houses the Office of the President (currently Farnam Jahanian, CMU's 10th president), the Office of Undergraduate Admission (2nd floor, walk-in M–F 8:30–4:30), the HUB on the lower level (CMU's one-stop enrollment center for financial aid, student accounts, registrar, and ID cards), and most senior administrative offices. A recent Landau Building Company renovation updated 42,011 sq ft across all six stories in under 8 months, bringing restrooms to ADA compliance and fully upgrading HVAC. The quiet treasure inside is the George Nakashima furniture collection — 60 pieces of master-craftsman Nakashima furniture commissioned 1965–1966 by interior designer Paul Planert for Warner's opening, gifted by the Scaife family. Iconic pieces including the Conoid Bench are still in active use in the President's and Admissions offices; it's one of the largest institutional Nakashima collections in the world and is featured on the Bloomberg Connects app. Every prospective student passes through: self-guided tour maps are available in the first-floor vestibules at both Warner and the Coulter Welcome Center, and enrolling students return to The HUB to pick up their CMU Student ID card. Out front on the lawn sits the iconic 100-foot stainless-steel "Walking to the Sky" sculpture by Jonathan Borofsky (CFA '64), installed May 2006 and donated by trustee Jill Gansman Kraus (A '74) and her husband Peter Kraus — a canonical campus photo spot. Fun techie detail: CMU's DNS LOC record geographically points to Warner Hall, making it the "official" location of cmu.edu on the internet.

CUC.title: Cohon University Center
summary: Jared L. Cohon University Center is our student union. Here students can take advantage of the student fitness facilities, catch a show at the black-box theater, visit the chapel, gather with other students in meeting rooms, or get lunch in one of many eateries.

You see our Scotty statue mascot that was funded and created by multiple CMU alumni. Our mascot is the Scottish Highland Terrier or Scottie for short. We like to call the dog “Scotty” who is a confident, independent and spirited breed. We students like to rub its nose for goodluck, so feel free to try that out before leaving this stop!

Additionally, located in this building is The Center for Student Diversity and Inclusion. The Center offers resources to enhance an inclusive and transformative student experience for our student population that joins us from 120 different countries. The Center is focused on access, success, campus climate and intergroup dialogue.

The Jared L. Cohon University Center is CMU's 24/7 student union, named in 2014 for 8th president Jared L. Cohon (1997–2013). Original building opened 1996 (Michael Dennis & Associates, postmodern echo of Hornbostel's Beaux-Arts); the 62,000-sq-ft expansion was designed by CannonDesign and built by Mosites Construction, opening May 2016 after a 19-month build, and winning the Master Builders' Association 2016 Building Excellence Award (New Construction $10–$25M) and an AIA Pennsylvania award. The new Lee Lobby features floor-to-ceiling windows, two native-plant rain gardens, and the signature art piece: Dale Chihuly's "Frank-Ratchye End of the Day Chandelier," a massive multi-colored blown-glass sculpture donated in 2013 by trustee Edward H. Frank and Sarah Ratchye to honor President Cohon, its colors symbolizing his commitment to diversity. Key spaces: McConomy Auditorium (445 seats, stadium-style), Rangos Ballroom (holds 450, dividable into three, hosts the Activities FAIR), Wiegand Gym, Maureen B. Cohon Cardio Fitness Center (10,000 sq ft), a 25-yard, 8-lane swimming pool (built 1996) with a separate diving well featuring two 1-meter and two 3-meter boards and a balcony seating up to 200 spectators, squash/racquetball courts, a Studio Theater black-box, a 24-hour multi-denominational prayer room, University Store, Art Store, and Tech Store. Dining is one of CMU's deepest lineups: Schatz Dining Room (campus's only all-you-care-to-eat buffet, 2nd floor), Au Bon Pain at Skibo Café, El Gallo de Oro (Mexican), Revolution Noodle (build-your-own Malatang noodle bowls, bao buns, bubble tea; opened 2022), Tazza D'Oro espresso, and Entropy+ convenience store. The Tartan Express food truck parks outside in Legacy Plaza. Outside in Merson Courtyard sits the bronze Scotty statue — CMU's Scottish terrier mascot — unveiled April 8, 2022 during Spring Carnival & Reunion Weekend, sculpted by alumnus Ray Kaskey (CFA) using a Scottish terrier named Bean as his model, and cast by Laran Bronze, a foundry owned by CFA alumnus Lawrence Welker. The statue's tail doubles as a handle so visitors can pull themselves up onto the granite base, which itself functions as a bench. It was funded by CFA alumna Kathy Sabec Dax and her late husband F. Robert Dax (a College of Engineering alumnus). The tradition is to rub Scotty's nose for good luck — and official CMU campus tours now conclude at the Scotty statue. The Scottish terrier became CMU's official mascot in 2007. The CUC hosts The FAIR (350+ student organizations), Late Night at CMU, orientation, and Spring Carnival events.

POS.title: Posner Hall
summary: Posner Hall is adjacent to the Hall of the Arts, which is home to some teaching and rehearsal spaces for the School of Music. This building is home to a student-favorite eatery called The Exchange as well as the Student Academic Success Center. The  Student Academic Success Center focuses on creating spaces for students to engage in their coursework and approach to learning through options like academic coaching, subject-specific tutoring, effective communication strategies, accommodations for students with disabilities, and language support for multilingual learners.

Built 1990–1993 as an expansion of the Graduate School of Industrial Administration by Kallmann McKinnell & Wood, Posner Hall was the original home of the Tepper School of Business until Tepper relocated to Tepper Quad in 2018. A full 2021 GBBN renovation (LEED Gold) repurposed the building for the Student Academic Success Center (1st floor), registrar classrooms, Dietrich College departments, and the Institute for Politics and Strategy. A gift of Henry Posner Jr. and his family. The star attraction is Kraus Campo (2005) — a rooftop garden-as-sculpture designed by conceptual artist Mel Bochner (CFA '62) — who died February 12, 2025 at 84 — with landscape architect Michael Van Valkenburgh, commissioned by trustee Jill Gansman Kraus (A'74). Features include a central 25-by-60-foot tile-covered platform shaped like a French curve and patterned with embedded black numbers in white tiles — a hallmark of Bochner's lifelong interest in numerical sequencing — winding orange pathways through plantings, and a 6-foot-by-58-foot tiled quotation — words referencing physicist Arthur Eddington on the second law of thermodynamics, attributed in context to Ludwig Wittgenstein, transcribed in reverse order as a literal visual puzzle that students walk past daily without ever quite finishing. Dining is The Exchange on the first floor — a 20-year CMU institution serving custom deli sandwiches (student favorite: "The Leonardo"), made-from-scratch soups, hot entrées, a salad bar, and La Prima coffee, sourced from local BreadWorks and Turner's Dairy Farm. The adjacent earth-sheltered Posner Center (2004, 11,400 sq ft) houses the Posner Memorial Collection of rare books and early calculating machines. In March 2025, the Posner Foundation committed $8 million to CMU Libraries Special Collections, funding a Perkins Eastman-designed renovation of the Posner Center scheduled to conclude fall 2025, reimagining it as "part museum, part laboratory for the humanities."

HWC.title: Highmark Center for Health, Wellness and Athletics
summary: The Highmark Center is a 160,000 square foot building recently opened which unifies robust health services, contemporary facilities and educational programs that support students’ minds, bodies and spirits in a comprehensive care model. It includes new full-service clinical areas as an expanded University Health Services; private and supportive spaces for Counseling and Psychological Services; and a modern athletics facility for practice, performance, training and athlete care.

Accuracy correction: the Highmark Center's cost is $105 million, not $200M+, per all official CMU sources. Groundbreaking was November 19, 2021; the building opened August 2024 for fall semester, with an official dedication October 24, 2024. 160,000 sq ft (142,000 new + 16,000 renovated) across four stories. Designed by Bohlin Cywinski Jackson, built in 36 months by Mascaro Construction, pursuing LEED Gold. The $35 million lead gift from Highmark, Inc. (Fall 2019) was one of the largest corporate partnerships in CMU history. Donor-named spaces include the Buncher Suite for Wellness, the Hoplamazian Family Well-Being Lab, the Rohr Intercollegiate Golf Training Facility, and the Block-Kelley Tartan Room. The building replaces the historic Skibo Gymnasium (1924), which hosted CMU's first basketball game (Feb. 5, 1924 vs. Pitt) and a Louis Armstrong performance. Skibo's core was preserved and woven into the new Center — its original exterior wall now lives inside as the secondary gym wall, 6,000 sq ft of salvaged wooden flooring appears in the Tartan Hall of Fame, the varsity weight room displays the original center-court Tartan logo, and copper feature walls are made from the patina-aged copper roofs of the old North Gym and Thistle Hall. Signature spaces: Main Arena (16,000 sq ft, seats ~1,000, home to varsity basketball and volleyball), secondary recreational gym (with six hoops, volleyball, three badminton courts, pickleball), Turf Fieldhouse inside Skibo's preserved shell (turf, running lanes, batting cages), Rohr Intercollegiate Golf Training Facility (three virtual training screens — used by the 2024 NCAA D-III Champion women's golf team), athletic training suite, student-athlete lounge. Upstairs: UHS clinic on the 3rd floor (with a juice bar), and CaPS counseling on the 4th floor with a Wellness Garden. The Buncher Suite includes four contemplation nooks, two ablution rooms, a gallery, and a circular Interfaith Room. UHS Wellness To Go vending machines provide on-site access to emergency contraception, sexual-health supplies, and OTC medications. Art includes Guadalupe Maravilla's Descansa Espíritus/Rest Spirits — six polished aluminum hammocks suspended as a symmetrical mobile, installed October 2024. Dining is Shake Smart — protein shakes, fruit smoothies, and açaí bowls. The Center is the first CMU facility to integrate physical health, mental health, spiritual life, and athletics under one roof, a model CMU positions as a national leader in holistic student wellness. It sits right next to Schenley Park.

FLD.title: Gesling Stadium
summary: Gesling Stadium (commonly nicknamed 'The G') is a 3,900-seat stadium located on Carnegie Mellon's campus at 5000 Forbes Avenue, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. It opened in 1990 as part of CMU's east campus project, which also included two new residence halls and a 700-space parking garage. CMU's official Athletics page lists the seating as 3,500 in the grandstands plus additional standing-room viewing.

The field at Gesling Stadium is officially dedicated to longtime Carnegie Mellon football head coach Rich Lackner, making the full name 'Richard M. Lackner Field at Gesling Stadium.' The naming was announced May 29, 2024 by the CMU Athletics Department in recognition of Lackner's coaching legacy.

The stadium is the home venue for the Carnegie Mellon Tartans varsity football team (fall season) and the men's and women's track and field teams (spring season). It also hosts club and intramural sports, including Rugby and Quidditch (Quadball). From 1990 to 2010 it additionally served as the home of CMU's varsity men's and women's soccer teams.

The playing surface is FieldTurf, originally installed in summer 2006 and most recently resurfaced in summer 2025. The infill mix uses silica sand and cryogenic rubber designed to emulate natural grass. The 8-lane running track encircling the field was resurfaced in summer 2016.

A state-of-the-art 13-foot by 24-foot video scoreboard was installed in 2019. The Jared L. Cohon University Center (CUC) forms the backdrop to the stadium's west end zone, while the Judith Resnik and West Wing residence halls overshadow the away sideline. Nearby dining facilities include the Carnegie Mellon Cafe (2006) and Tartans Pavilion (2007).

Despite Carnegie Mellon competing at the NCAA Division III level (in the Presidents' Athletic Conference), Gesling Stadium is notable for being the largest stadium in the city of Pittsburgh purpose-built primarily for college football. The University of Pittsburgh's Panthers (Division I) play at Acrisure Stadium, which was primarily built for the NFL Pittsburgh Steelers; the Duquesne Dukes' Arthur J. Rooney Athletic Field has a capacity of only 2,200.

WTS.title: Walking to the Sky
summary: Walking to the Sky is a 100-foot-tall stainless steel sculpture by Jonathan Borofsky (CMU College of Fine Arts, 1964), installed on CMU's campus in May 2006. The tapered pole leans at a 75-degree angle and is roughly the width of two flagpoles. Ten realistically painted life-size figures populate the piece — seven climbing the pole and three standing at its base — representing people of all ages, races, and walks of life ascending together.

Borofsky has said the work was inspired by childhood stories his father told him about a friendly giant living in the sky, and that it celebrates "the human potential for discovering who we are and where we need to go" — all of humanity rising upwards from the earth to the heavens above. The sculpture was donated by CMU trustee Jill Gansman Kraus (A '74) and her husband Peter Kraus. It stands on the lawn at Warner Hall just off Forbes Avenue, and is one of the most photographed spots on campus.

FENCE.title: The Fence
summary: The Fence is one of CMU's most beloved traditions and is widely considered the most painted object in the world. Originally a wooden footbridge railing built in 1916, it has been continuously painted by student groups for over a century to advertise events, celebrate milestones, and share messages with the community.

Tradition dictates that the Fence can only be painted between midnight and sunrise, by hand using a brush, and a group must be present to guard it 24/7 in order to keep it. By 1993, layers of paint had grown so heavy that the original Fence collapsed under its own weight; the current concrete and steel structure was built to carry the legacy forward.
